title: How We Saw God’s Goodness Through Our Child’s Cancer
summary: It was not in the good moments where God’s care was most evident. It was in the dark moments, often at night, when we were unsure if our son would survive.
summary_zh: 这不是在神的关怀最明显的美好时刻。在黑暗的时刻，通常是在晚上，我们不确定我们的儿子是否能活下来。
title_zh: 我们如何从孩子的癌症中看到神的良善
content: To encounter profound suffering is to wrestle with isolation. From Job’s seat in the ashes to your neighbor’s loss, news of suffering often includes a struggle to connect. Our family’s cancer journey was like that. We felt alone. And we sensed disconnection—even helplessness—from people who heard the news. Childhood cancer is a blessedly uncommon experience, but navigating pain is inherent to life in a fallen world. When we encounter others’ pain, we have a “Good Samaritan choice”—to step forward and show compassion or to walk away. Nightmare Our 3-year-old son, Ben, had an unexplained illness. After a week in the hospital, we were ushered into an ICU conference room full of doctors and nurses. They delivered the news: “Your son has cancer.” One of the nurses was crying before they even said a word. Our family is from Washington, DC, but we were about 10,000 miles from home. We’d been serving as missionaries in Costa Rica, yet we weren’t there either. On that January day, we were in a hospital in Sydney, Australia, on our dream trip—a family Christmas in summertime. It was quickly becoming a nightmare. The days after the diagnosis were filled with rapid changes. We couldn’t go back to Costa Rica. Returning to DC was almost impossible. The Ronald McDonald House was our new home. My daughter started kindergarten at a new school, in a new country. She drew a picture of her family. There was no home, garden, or pets—just a hospital bed. Ben on his last day of chemotherapy / Courtesy of Peter Morris Over the next six months, Ben endured 96 nights in the hospital, 25 general anesthetics, and chemotherapy so strong it could blind or even kill an adult. He was traveling through the metaphorical valley of the shadow of death, and it was decorated with bright colors and superhero stickers. May 22 is a day we still celebrate in our family as “no more chemo day.” Ben took his final dose of chemotherapy, and we rejoiced with a trip to McDonald’s and a chocolate cake. Despite the celebration, the years ahead held mortal peril. His doctor told us relapse was a risk without a treatment plan. All we could do was watch and wait. Ben was immunocompromised for the years that followed, extending into the 2020s when the disruption of a health crisis—previously rare—became globally mundane. Today, Ben’s body still carries the scars of his cancer and the side effects of the lifesaving treatment he received. But he’s a survivor. To any passerby, he looks like an ordinary 12-year-old boy. My wife and I have scars too. But we also carry the lessons the Lord taught us along the way. Those lessons are available to all believers as we encounter the pain of others. Here are three that stand out. 1. You can’t depend on people. Suffering has an odd way of resetting relationships. We saw it repeatedly, in our experience and with other cancer families we met. The apparent uniqueness of the suffering—and the emotional reactions it stirred—drove some people away. They wouldn’t, or couldn’t, step close and walk with us. However, those people stepping away opened the door to gospel opportunities for us. Australian hospitals rarely have private rooms, so we spent most of our 96 nights sharing rooms with people from diverse cultures and faiths. As other people pulled back from them, we were able to step forward and hold out the hope of the gospel in a dark and hopeless place. 2. You can depend on people. While some in our life pulled away, others chose to pull close. We were thousands of miles from our church family, but people still found ways to care for us. When we shared the news about Ben’s illness, our Facebook post reached more than 15,000 people around the world. It wasn’t the eyeballs that made a difference but the thoughtful actions. title: When Morningness Is Confused with Godliness
summary: Could it be possible that our idealizing of morning quiet times is more cultural than biblical?
summary_zh: 我们对早晨安静时间的理想化是否比圣经更具文化性？
title_zh: 当早晨与虔诚混淆时
content: “Do your quiet time with God every morning.” “Give God your first hours (your best hours!) of the day.” “Rise early for Scripture and prayer; it sets the tone for the rest of your day!” From pulpits to podcasts, I’ve heard these sentiments often in Christian circles. The instructions aren’t just to spend alone time with God but to specifically do so as the very first act of your day. For many, the “morning quiet time” has become a measuring rod of how well you’re doing in your relationship with God. Actor Mark Wahlberg once went viral on Instagram for a screenshot of his morning routine : waking up at 2:30 a.m., praying at 2:45, and completing his first workout before 5:30. This is one of many examples of how early rising has become associated with aspirational godliness. But is it really more virtuous to be a morning person than a night owl? What If You Have to Sleep In? Behind the modern mindset of hyperidealized mornings is the assumption that being a “morning person” is a virtue in and of itself—a gritty choice toward wellness and productivity within everyone’s power. The implication is that if you’re disciplined and wise, you’ll set the alarm clock and start the day early; you’ll make it happen. If you’re slothful or foolish, you won’t. Extenuating circumstances are just excuses. For many, the ‘morning quiet time’ has become a measuring rod of how well you’re doing in your relationship with God. But what would this mean for nurses whose work begins and ends when it’s dark outside? What about parents with newborns, whose babies’ demands don’t abide by our ideal rhythms? How about Christians who are naturally night owls: most alert, focused, and productive at night? Should these folks just suck it up and aspire to get up earlier in spite of their circumstances? Or could it be possible that our idealizing of morning quiet times is more cultural than biblical? God Loves Early Risers At first glance, it might seem that God’s Word does value our mornings most. Pastor David Mathis wrote an insightful article summarizing the abundance of instances in Scripture in which God’s people (including Christ himself!) either rose early to good effect or were directed by God to do so. Consider the Psalms: In Psalm 5:3, David says, “O LORD, in the morning you hear my voice.” In Psalm 88:13, the Sons of Korah sing, “In the morning my prayer comes before you.” In Psalm 90:14, Moses prays to God, “Satisfy us in the morning with your steadfast love, that we may rejoice and be glad all our days.” God clearly meets with his people in the morning. Case closed? Not quite. When you consult the whole counsel of Scripture, it becomes clear that God emphasizes meditating on his Word, singing his praises, and praying to his name just as much in the night as in the morning. In Acts 16:25–26, after Paul and Silas are imprisoned in Philippi, God’s Word notably mentions the timing of their worship: “About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God . . .” Silas and Paul don’t try to go to sleep early so they can engage with God at the crack of dawn. They stay up late, worshiping at midnight. The results are profound. In Psalm 63:5–6, David prays to the Lord, “My soul will be satisfied as with fat and rich food, and my mouth will praise you with joyful lips, when I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night.” This psalm as a whole is arguably a nighttime prayer. David prays these lyrics to the Lord seemingly all while on his “bed,” singing midnight praises. Consider Jesus’s earthly life. On the fateful day before his crucifixion, when it comes to spending devoted time alone with his Father, Jesus prays passionately, in Gethsemane, at night (Matt. 26:36–56). content: On Nov. 6, Titus Hassan Malika stood with his classmates and received his diploma — a quiet but powerful moment marking the end of a long, difficult road. The Sudanese Christian, who fled violence and persecution in his homeland, had received support from International Christian Concern (ICC). With God’s help, what once seemed impossible had become reality. “The support I received from ICC is a dream come true,” Malika said. “I never imagined that someone would stand with me for so many years, believing in my future when I could barely see it myself. This graduation is not only my achievement — it is the fruit of their faithfulness and God’s provision.” Titus grew up in Sudan, where following Jesus grew increasingly dangerous . As pressure on Christian communities intensified amid conflict and targeted hostility, he was forced to leave everything behind. With little more than his faith, he crossed into Kenya as a refugee, carrying the weight of loss, uncertainty, and the hope that God still had a future for him. By His Side In 2023, ICC stepped into that uncertainty. Through consistent support, practical help, encouragement, and the means to continue his studies, we walked with Titus through years of hardship. The path was not easy. He faced the daily challenges of life, the lingering trauma of persecution, and the enduring discipline of education while far from home. Yet he pressed on. “Jesus Christ has been the center of my life from the day I fled Sudan until this moment,” he said. “When I had no home, he was my shelter. When fear tried to silence me, he gave me courage. Every step of this journey has been possible only because he walked with me and never left me alone.” As he steps into his next chapter, Titus carries both a Bachelor’s degree in business administration and management, as well as a testimony that God can bring beauty from ashes, and that the Body of Christ, when it stands with the persecuted, can help rewrite a life marked by suffering into one marked by grace. “I give thanks to God for ICC, for they have been the hands and feet of Christ to me,” he said. “As it is written, ‘And my God will meet all your needs according to the riches of his glory in Christ Jesus’ (Philippians 4:19). Truly, the Lord has done this. May he continue to bless those who have poured out their lives so that I could stand here today.” To read more news stories, visit the ICC Newsroom . For interviews, please email us . To support ICC’s work around the world, please give to our Where Most Needed Fund . content: Suspected Muslim Gunmen killed at least six people, including a Nigerian soldier, in separate attacks on communities in Plateau state, Nigeria. The attacks occurred on Sunday night, Nov. 8, in Bel village, Sho community, Barkin Ladi Local Government Area (LGA), and Lakas community in Panyam, near the Mangu-Pankshin border in Mangu LGA. Four people, including three civilians and a soldier, were reportedly killed when gunmen stormed Bel village at about 9 p.m. and opened fire. A resident of Bel village, Bulus Bot, who confirmed the attack to International Christian Concern (ICC), said several people also sustained gunshot injuries. The attack forced residents to seek safety as gunfire rang through the community. He said the attackers are Islamic Fulani herders who want to take over their land. Rwang Tengwong, publicity secretary of the Berom Youth Moulders Association (BYM), confirmed the killings and identified three of the civilian victims as Emmanuel Pam Dachung, 15; Joseph Gyang, 28; and Emmanuel Yohanna, 32. The soldier has not been publicly identified. According to a six-year study conducted by the Observatory for Religious Freedom in Africa (ORFA), Islamic Fulani militias are by far the deadliest persecutors of Christians in Nigeria. The network of militias is responsible for four times more civilian deaths than the two prominent Islamic terror organizations, Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), combined. The study’s findings challenge the commonly held belief that the two organized terror groups kill the larger number of Christians, highlighting the Fulani network’s expanded efforts to target Christians. A Second Attack Two additional people were reportedly killed in a separate attack on the Lakas community in Panyam, bringing the reported death toll from the two incidents to at least six. “Muslim Fulani stopped us from going to the farm to harvest our crops, and we are now afraid to go to the church to worship,” Mathias said. “Nigerian authorities failed to protect us.” Tengwong told ICC that no arrests had been made following either attack. He specifically accused the Nigerian Army of failing to apprehend any of the suspected Fulani attackers. Tengwong condemned the killings and called on security agencies to identify and arrest those responsible, warning that the failure to apprehend attackers could leave surrounding communities exposed to further violence. Residents and eyewitnesses alleged that Fulani extremists carried out the attacks, targeting predominantly Christian communities. Some residents described the assaults as part of a pattern of violence aimed at taking over ancestral lands and forcing indigenous populations from their communities. These allegations could not be independently verified. The latest attacks add to continuing reports of armed assaults against rural communities in Plateau, particularly in Barkin Ladi, Bassa, Riyom, and Mangu local government areas, where Christian farming communities have repeatedly reported killings, destruction of property, displacement, and threats to their livelihoods. 据报,有4人,包括3名平民和1名士兵,在晚上9时左右枪手冲进Bel村并开火时被打死。 Bel村的一名居民Bulus Bot向国际基督教关注组织证实这次袭击,他说,一些人也遭到枪伤。 袭击迫使居民在枪声响彻社区时寻求安全。

他说袭击者是伊斯兰富拉尼牧民,他们想占领他们的土地. 贝罗姆青年穆尔德斯协会(BYM)宣传秘书Rwang Tengwong证实了这些杀人事件,并指认了3名平民受害者:15岁的Emmanuel Pam Dachung;28岁的Joseph Gyang;32岁的Emmanuel Yohanna。 该士兵尚未公开确认身份。

根据非洲宗教自由观察站(ORFA)进行的一项为期六年的研究,伊斯兰富拉尼民兵是尼日利亚基督教徒最致命的迫害者。 民兵网络造成平民死亡的人数是博科圣地和西非伊斯兰国省这两个著名的伊斯兰恐怖组织的四倍。

研究结论质疑人们的普遍看法,即两个有组织的恐怖集团杀害了更多的基督徒,突出了富拉尼网络扩大针对基督徒的努力。 第二次攻击 据报告,在对Panyam的Lakas社区进行的另一次袭击中,又有两人丧生,据报这两起事件的死亡人数至少达6人。

Mathias说:“穆斯林Fulani阻止我们去农场收获作物, “尼日利亚当局未能保护我们。” Tengwong告诉国际刑事法院,在两次袭击之后都没有逮捕任何人。 他具体指责尼日利亚军队没有逮捕任何涉嫌的Fulani袭击者。

Tengwong谴责这些杀人事件,呼吁安全机构查明并逮捕肇事者,并警告说,不逮捕袭击者可能会使周围的社区面临进一步的暴力。 居民和目击者指称,Fulani极端分子进行攻击,攻击目标主要是基督教社区。

content: In early October, a 20-year-old Coptic Christian was kidnapped and killed at the hands of the Islamic State group. Milad Malak lived in Sebarbay, Egypt, and served as a church deacon at a local Coptic church. However, because of the country’s economic decline, he traveled to Libya on Sept. 2 to find work. He made a day’s journey with two Muslim friends and arrived in Zliten, where they stayed with other Egyptian migrant workers. On the morning of Oct. 4, ISIS militants kidnapped them. The captors subjected the group to abuse while they held them hostage for ransom money. Milad’s friends were released after their families paid a $4,700 ransom. They are now receiving medical treatment at a hospital in Egypt. Milad’s sister, Madonna Malek, told Worthy News that their family paid a ransom, but because he was the only Christian in the group, his kidnappers refused to release him and violently pressured him to convert to Islam. Milad stood strong in his faith until the end. He told his persecutors, “Even if you cut me into pieces, I would never renounce my faith.” When the militants realized they could not force him to abandon his God, they killed him. Faithful Until the End After hearing about his death from his friends, Milad’s family appealed to the Egyptian government, asking them to intervene and demand that his body be returned home. Several weeks went by until it was finally released, and on Oct. 28, grieving family members and fellow Christians gathered to celebrate the life of their beloved son and friend. “He was faithful to Christ till his last breath,” a family friend said. Open Doors ranked Libya as the ninth most dangerous place to be a Christian. A Muslim-majority nation, Christians face heavy pressure to abandon their faith. Milad’s death has reminded believers of the massacre that occurred in 2015, when 20 Coptic Christians and one Ghanaian were beheaded by militants in Libya for standing strong in their faith. Milad joins them as yet another martyr who inspires Christians worldwide to be bold witnesses for Christ until the very end. Story by Bella Agnello To read more news stories, visit the ICC Newsroom . 他们目前正在埃及的一家医院接受治疗。 米拉德的妹妹麦当娜·马利克(Madonna Malek)告诉沃西新闻,他们的家人支付了赎金,但由于他是这群人中唯一的基督徒,绑匪拒绝释放他,并用暴力逼迫他皈依伊斯兰教. 米拉德坚守信仰,直到最后.

他对他的迫害者说:即使你把我割成碎片,我也不会放弃我的信仰。 当激进分子意识到他们不能强迫他放弃上帝时,他们杀了他. Milad的家人在从朋友那里得知他的死讯后,

content: By ICC Fellow Lisa Navarrette For years, Fadi has told his children the same thing: We stay. He is a Christian father in Lebanon. His family has lived in the same town for generations, and his parents are buried nearby. Fadi’s children were baptized in the church where he married his wife, Nour. His small business survived political unrest, the economic collapse, the Beirut port explosion, and another round of regional conflict. Leaving always felt like surrender. But lately, the calculation has changed. Fuel costs have risen again. Groceries take a larger share of the family’s income. Electricity is unreliable, so the business depends partly on a generator. Transportation costs more. His oldest daughter has been accepted to a university abroad, while his younger son talks openly about finding work in Europe. One evening, Fadi places two folders on the kitchen table. One contains bills. The other contains immigration documents. “We don’t have to decide tonight,” she said. Fadi looks at the paperwork for a long time. Years earlier, violence made the family afraid to leave home. Now economics is making them wonder whether they should leave the country. That is the final link in the chain this series examines. Fighting to Stay High fuel prices do not create religious persecution. But when families have already endured violence, displacement, discrimination, destroyed livelihoods, or political instability, rising energy costs can make recovery harder and staying less sustainable. In 2026, the World Bank warned that the Middle East conflict had created a major energy shock, raising fuel prices, increasing inflation, disrupting transportation and logistics, and weakening economic growth. Its October 2026 regional economic update found that fragile and conflict-affected economies were experiencing especially severe pressure , with poverty still rising in parts of the region even as it declined elsewhere. Those regional trends eventually become household questions: Can the business stay open? Can the family still afford food? Will there be jobs for the children? Is rebuilding worth the cost? Lebanon illustrates how those pressures can accumulate. Christians there have not experienced the same mass expulsion seen in parts of Iraq or Syria, but International Christian Concern (ICC) has documented how economic collapse, political instability, regional conflict, and emigration continue to weaken one of the Middle East’s most important Christian communities. No single crisis explains why a family leaves. That is what makes the process easy to overlook. A Christian family may survive violence but lose its savings. It may survive political instability but lose its business. It may rebuild after displacement only to discover that electricity, fuel, food, and transportation have become increasingly expensive. Eventually, the question is no longer only whether the family is safe. It is whether the family can build a future. Affording Daily Life The same dynamic is evident in Syria, where many people have tried to return after years of war. In May 2026, ICC reported that about 1.67 million refugees and 1.9 million internally displaced Syrians had returned since December 2024. Yet the agency warned that damaged housing, limited livelihoods, weak infrastructure, poverty, and restricted access to basic services continued to threaten the sustainability of those returns. A separate 2026 assessment hosted by UNHCR reached a similar conclusion : whether people remain after returning depends heavily on housing, employment, services, and economic opportunity. For Christian communities, that distinction matters. Imagine a family returning to a Syrian town after years abroad. They repair part of their home. Their children reenter school. The father begins rebuilding a small business. Then expenses start adding up. Electricity remains unreliable. Fuel for the generator costs more. 由ICC研究员莉萨·纳瓦雷特(Lisa Navarrette) 多年来,法迪对他的孩子说了同样的话:我们留下。 他是黎巴嫩的基督教父亲. 他的家族世代居住在同一个城镇,父母也葬在附近. Fadi的孩子在与妻子Nour结婚的教堂接受洗礼。

他的小企业在政治动荡,经济崩溃,贝鲁特港口爆炸以及另一轮区域冲突中幸存下来. 离开总是觉得投降。 但最近,计算方式发生了变化。 燃料成本再次上升。 食谱占家庭收入的较大份额。 电力不可靠,因此业务部分依赖于发电机. 运输成本更高。

他的大女儿被录取到国外的一所大学,而小儿子则公开谈论在欧洲找工作. 一天晚上,法迪把两个文件夹放在厨房桌子上. 一个有账单。 另一个文件载有移民证件。 “我们不必在今晚决定, 法迪很长一段时间都在看文件 几年前,暴力使家庭不敢离家。

现在经济学让他们怀疑他们是否应该出国。 这是本系列审查的链条的最后环节。 高油价斗争不会造成宗教迫害。

但是,当家庭已经忍受了暴力、流离失所、歧视、生计被摧毁或政治不稳定时,能源成本的上升会使恢复更加困难,并降低可持续性。

2026年,世界银行警告说,中东冲突造成了严重的能源冲击,燃料价格上涨,通货膨胀加剧,交通和后勤中断,经济增长减弱.

其2026年10月的区域经济最新情况发现,脆弱和受冲突影响的经济体正承受着特别严重的压力,该区域部分地区的贫困现象仍在加剧,尽管其他地区的贫困状况有所下降。 这些区域趋势最终成为家庭问题:企业能否继续开放? 家人还能买得起食物吗? 孩子们会有工作吗?

重建值得付出代价吗? 黎巴嫩说明了这些压力如何能够累积。 但国际基督教关注组织(ICC)记录了经济崩溃、政治不稳定、地区冲突和移民继续削弱中东最重要的基督教社区之一。

没有一个危机能解释一个家庭为什么离开。 这使得这一进程容易被忽视。 一个基督教家庭可能会在暴力中幸存下来,但却会失去积蓄。 它可能在政治不稳定的情况下生存下来,但失去了业务。 它可能在流离失所后重建,只为了发现电力、燃料、粮食和交通越来越昂贵。

最后,问题不再仅仅是家庭是否安全。 家庭是否能够建立未来。 每日生活 同样的动态在叙利亚也很明显,许多人在多年战争之后试图返回叙利亚。 2026年5月,国际刑事法院报告说,自2024年12月以来,约有167万难民和190万境内流离失所的叙利亚人返回。

然而,该机构警告说,住房受损、生计有限、基础设施薄弱、贫穷以及获得基本服务的机会有限,继续威胁着这些回返的可持续性。 难民署主办的2026年的单独评估得出了类似结论:人们返回后是否仍留在当地,在很大程度上取决于住房、就业、服务和经济机会。

对基督教社区来说,这种区别很重要。 想象一个家庭在海外多年后返回叙利亚城镇。 他们修补了一部分家 他们的孩子重新入学。 父亲开始重建小生意. 然后费用开始增加。 电力仍然不可靠。 发电机的燃料成本更高。 工作和上学的交通占收入的较大份额。

He reflected, “I think when you’re raised in a Christian home … and you have the routines of a life that is built around church and prayer, you just take it for granted.” He added, “It was just the air I breathed.” For Ken and his wife, Sally, faith was always part of their stories. They were each raised in Christian homes, followed Christ, got baptized and had parents who faithfully modeled church attendance, prayer and generosity.  Ken and Sally’s paths eventually crossed at Greenville University in southern Illinois, where they met and fell in love. They went on to build a life centered around family, faith and service. Ken spent his career as a teacher and coach while Sally worked as an accountant, and together they raised two children. Now retired, they’ve moved to be closer to their children and grandchildren, giving them a new opportunity to pour into the next generation. Early in their marriage, Ken and Sally met a mentor who encouraged the couple to go deeper with their faith — to study Scripture, ask questions and wrestle honestly with what they believed. It was an important season of discovering that the faith that had been passed down from their families could also become something they personally owned and lived out together. title: Finding Wonder in the Midst of Christmas Weariness

summary: Rediscover the wonder of Christmas by focusing on God’s faithfulness and the hope found in Jesus.   The post  Finding Wonder in the Midst of Christmas Weariness  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
summary_zh: 通过关注神的信实和耶稣的盼望，重新发现圣诞节的奇迹。“在圣诞节疲惫中寻找奇迹”一文首次出现在威克里夫。
title_zh: 在圣诞节疲惫中寻找奇迹
content: Christmas is supposed to be a season of wonder. Twinkling lights, familiar songs, meaningful traditions and time with people you love can all point toward the joy of celebrating Jesus’ birth. But when your December calendar fills with responsibilities and expectations, weariness can settle in before you realize it. Maybe you remember a time when Christmas felt different. As a child, you may have counted down the days and experienced joy in even the smallest traditions. As an adult, you might find yourself simply trying to catch your breath as you move from one responsibility to the next. In the middle of trying to make Christmas special for everyone else, it can be easy to miss the wonder yourself. But the Christmas story gives you an opportunity to slow down and remember what this season is really about. In Luke 1, before the story of Jesus’ birth begins, you meet people who knew what it meant to wait, wonder and trust that God was at work even when they couldn’t yet see what He was doing. Weary of Waiting Luke’s account of the life of Jesus doesn’t begin with Jesus’ birth; it begins instead with the story of Zechariah, an elderly priest who was tired of waiting. Zechariah had heard promises of Israel’s rescue from oppression and sin his entire life. That future must have seemed out of reach under Rome’s harsh control. But Zechariah and his wife, Elizabeth, also had an unfulfilled personal longing: “They had no children because Elizabeth was unable to conceive, and they were both very old” ( Luke 1:7, NLT ). One day, as Zechariah performed his duties in the temple, he was chosen to burn incense in the sanctuary — a rare honor with an unexpected result: While Zechariah was in the sanctuary, an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing to the right of the incense altar. Zechariah was shaken and overwhelmed with fear when he saw him. But the angel said, “Don’t be afraid, Zechariah! God has heard your prayer. Your wife, Elizabeth, will give you a son, and you are to name him John. You will have great joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth, for he will be great in the eyes of the Lord. He must never touch wine or other alcoholic drinks. He will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even before his birth. And he will turn many Israelites to the Lord their God. He will be a man with the spirit and power of Elijah. He will prepare the people for the coming of the Lord. He will turn the hearts of the fathers to their children, and he will cause those who are rebellious to accept the wisdom of the godly” ( Luke 1:11-17, NLT ). Trusting God in the Waiting An angel of the Lord appeared to Zechariah and announced that God had heard his prayer. Elizabeth would have a son named John who would “… prepare the people for the coming of the Lord” ( Luke 1:17b, NLT ). After years of waiting, God answered Zechariah and Elizabeth’s prayer as part of an even bigger story: They would finally have the child they had prayed for, and their son would prepare the way for Jesus. But Zechariah struggled to understand how it could possibly happen: “… ‘How can I be sure this will happen? I’m an old man now, and my wife is also well along in years’” ( Luke 1:18, NLT ). Zechariah could only see what seemed possible based on his circumstances. But God was asking him to trust what He had promised. The angel Gabriel responded by telling Zechariah that he would be unable to speak until the child was born, adding, “For my words will certainly be fulfilled at the proper time” ( Luke 1:20b, NLT ). Maybe you know what it’s like to pray about something for months or even years. It can be hard to keep trusting that God is working when it seems like nothing is changing. Zechariah’s story reminds us that even when we can’t see what God is doing, He is still faithful to His promises. Waiting is woven throughout the Christmas story. Maybe it’s part of your story too. Maybe the previous reader has ripped out a page, the series was canceled before the showrunners could wrap up the plotline, or the producer distributed the episode before realizing it was incomplete. How incredibly frustrating to not experience the full story from start to finish! It can leave us emotionally unsettled, frustrated or even distraught, because at our core, we desire completion. We want to know how things start and how they end. We don’t just want a taste, because it feels like a tease. We’re left wanting more . And we’re not alone in that desire! The same is true for communities around the world who are still waiting for the full counsel of God’s Word in a language and format they clearly understand. For some, they’re still waiting for the first verse of Scripture to be translated into their language. Others might have a few verses, chapters or Scripture portions . Still others are blessed with a complete New Testament but are waiting for the Old Testament so they can understand everything from Genesis to Revelation. They get a teaser of God’s great story — perhaps enough to understand who Jesus is and that He died for them — but they don’t have the full context as to why His sacrifice was so significant. content: How old were you when you first learned that Jesus loves you? Perhaps you’ve always known it and can’t remember a day when you didn’t know the song “Jesus Loves Me” or couldn’t recite John 3:16 by heart. Maybe you were a teenager and learned about Jesus’ love through a friend or church summer camp. Or were in college and went to a concert where the gospel was clearly articulated. Maybe you were in the trenches of the workforce, and a coworker boldly shared with you about the God who radically changed their life. Regardless of how old you were, each of us who has chosen to follow Jesus has an origin story — a moment in our lives when the knowledge that “Jesus loves me, this I know, for the Bible tells me so” moved from head knowledge to heart belief. And from then on, our lives were transformed forever. This is the truth of the gospel and the power of understanding that Jesus loves you. People around the world are discovering the personal truth of John 3:16 for themselves in a language and format they clearly understand. Stories were told and retold, Scripture was translated, churches were planted, and discipleship deepened as people learned more about Jesus. Bible translation is foundational to all ministries of the church. It fuels evangelism, church planting, discipleship and more. It equips people to move from a blurry picture of who God is to a clear understanding and personal encounter with Jesus as Lord. Through Scripture, people are able to read, hear or see the love of God on display. Just two decades ago, most of the world’s language communities still needed Bible translation work to begin , let alone be completed. But praise God, in the last few years, we’ve seen tremendous progress made, with Bible translation underway in more languages than ever before . While the change in numbers is exciting, what’s more important is what they signify: Every number represents a person who has a story that matters to God. content: What circumstances or experiences have shaped your life? For 93-year-old Millie (name changed), her testimony was shaped by the Great Depression and deep loss, but also by an enduring faith and a lifetime of seeing God’s faithfulness unfold. Every chapter of her story points back to the same truth: God’s Word sustained her. Millie was only six weeks old when her father suffered severe burns to his legs from an explosion. Overnight, Millie’s mother found herself caring for a newborn and a toddler while tending to a husband who was facing a long and painful recovery. Life was uncertain, and every dollar mattered. Yet when Millie looks back on those difficult years, she doesn’t first remember hardship. She remembers the faith that was demonstrated. Every Sunday morning, Millie’s mother would reach into a small jar where she saved a few quarters and hand one to Millie and one to her sister before they left for church. The family didn’t have much, but her parents believed that honoring God was never dependent on how much they had. “We were taught to tithe,” Millie recalled. “To give to the Lord because of His goodness to us.” Long before Millie understood phrases like “stewardship” or “planned giving,” she was learning a lesson that would shape the rest of her life: Generosity isn’t born out of abundance; it grows from trusting the one who provides. See how God is using the generosity of one group of friends to impact Bible translation → The Scripture Millie Carried Through the Years As Millie grew older, that foundation of faith continued to guide her. She married a godly man, and they centered their efforts around family, teaching and serving others. Both were educators, and they poured themselves into the lives of children while also remaining deeply involved in their church and community. Together, the couple experienced the joys of raising a family. But they also walked through a devastating loss. While Millie was pregnant with their younger son, the couple’s 7-year-old daughter tragically died. It’s difficult to imagine the depth of grief that Millie endured. Through her pain, she turned to God and His Word for comfort. Even now, decades later, she is still anchored by the promises found in Scripture. One particular passage resonates with Millie deeply: You will keep in perfect peace all who trust in you, all whose thoughts are fixed on you! Trust in the LORD always, for the LORD GOD is the eternal Rock. — Isaiah 26:3-4 (NLT) For Millie, Scripture was what met her in her grief, strengthened her through suffering and continued to anchor and guide her throughout the next chapters of her life. Millie believes the Lord’s presence was unmistakable in the moments that followed this event. For our ongoing series of feature articles for pastors and Christian leaders, we asked Dieudonné Tamfu (PhD, Southern Baptist Theological Seminary), pastor of Église Baptiste Bethléem and Assistant Professor of Bible and Theology and Director of the Cameroon Extension Site of Bethlehem College and Seminary, to introduce readers to the recently published Africa Statement on the Prosperity Gospel and Word of Faith Theology . Christian leadership is war. When God calls a man to shepherd his flock, he calls him to war against wolves. Satan, the father of lies, and his minions hate the spiritual health of God’s people, wanting nothing more than to lead the people of God from truth to idolatry. The spiritual leaders of God’s flock are called to fight against Satan’s counterfeit gospels by proclaiming the word of God (Ephesians 6:17). When those leaders fall silent, when they fail to preach the sufficiency of Christ alone, they make space for Satan to lead the people of God into idolatry. As John Calvin rightly said, “Those in authority in the church turned over to idols the office of teaching for no other reason than that they themselves were mute.” 1 The muteness of faithful leaders gives voices to idols. Since Genesis 3, the devil has been in the business of poisoning the minds of God’s people with lies. In God’s good garden, the enemy came preaching lies: If God truly loves you, he will give you the fruit from the tree in the middle of the garden. Eve paid close attention while Adam idly stood by, mute. Thus he, his wife, and all his descendants died of the poison of Satan. The world is under the curse of sin because of a failure of leadership. 2 One of Satan’s most deceptive counterfeits plaguing both American and African churches is the prosperity gospel, a false teaching that elevates the idols of health, wealth, and power. David Oyedepo, a strong proponent of the prosperity gospel and word-of-faith theology, says, “Healing is the covenant right of every child of God . . . sickness has no right to feast on your life.” He goes on to proclaim healing over his congregation: “In the name of Jesus, I decree an end to every toil with sickness and disease.” He assures them that faith in Jesus means the end of sickness. 3 As I’ve written elsewhere, this “idolatrous perversion of the gospel” turns Jesus into “a means to God’s full blessings, primarily of health, wealth, and might” in the present life. 4 Its widespread success indicates a failure on the part of so-called shepherds to engage in spiritual warfare by speaking the whole testimony of God’s word. Today, many church leaders in Africa are boldly refusing to remain mute while the “new serpent,” the prosperity gospel and word-of-faith theology, reinterpret God’s goodness as mere material blessings. These bold leaders are now advancing the centrality of the true gospel by the recent publication of the Africa Statement on the Prosperity Gospel and Word of Faith Theology . title: ‘Young Man, You Look Miserable’
summary: God changed the heart of a young “prince of preachers” all with a single, simple verse: Look to Jesus and live. Watch Now

title_zh: ‘年轻人，你看起来很悲惨’
content: I’m excited to tell you the story of how God used a simple verse, from a complicated passage, to change the life of a man named Charles Spurgeon. His story is for everyone, but it may have a special word to speak to a few groups in the room. One is laymen — that is, people who work for a living in normal jobs, outside of Christian ministry. People without a seminary education, people who aren’t pastors or have ministry jobs. We recognize that this series has profiled four men who were preachers. Now, there is an interesting flow to our series: - first, Saint Augustine, - then, Luther, who was an Augustinian monk, - then, John Bunyan, whose favorite book outside the Bible was Luther’s commentary on Galatians, - now, Charles Spurgeon, whose favorite book outside the Bible was Bunyan’s Pilgrim’s Progress. We’ve moved from one convert to another, each building in some way on the previous one, but a weakness of our series (in some sense) is that they all became preachers. And we don’t expect you all to become preachers; we’d like a few, but most will be laymen, and that’s good. Now, Spurgeon is known as “the Prince of Preachers.” But the hero, under God, in Spurgeon’s story is not Spurgeon, and not a trained, paid preacher, but a layman. So, Spurgeon’s story has a special word for laymen who are willing to open their mouths and say what they know about Jesus. Spurgeon’s story also has a special word for teens and young adults. Spurgeon came to faith at age fifteen, which in his day was far more like young adulthood. Still, his story offers a challenge to those who are no longer children and not yet established adults: teens, college students, grad students, even young professionals. Don’t let the world (or the church) lower your standards of what’s possible in being deeply converted and dedicated to Jesus — and how God can make his Son thrilling to a young soul. My prayer is that God might be pleased to give some their own engine. So often, parents, college workers, and pastors help young adults along and give them pushes. And then sometimes, God is pleased in the life of teenagers to give them their own engine, and they don’t need any more pushing. They say, “Get out of my way! I am going to follow Jesus. You can’t keep me from him and worship, my Bible, and prayer!” That’s what God did for Spurgeon at age fifteen — he gave him his own engine. And I pray he might be pleased to do that even here this morning. Spurgeon’s story speaks to one more group: those in the room who are willing to admit, “I’m here but I’m not saved.” For two thousand years, unsaved people have shown up at churches for all sorts of reasons. That’s Spurgeon’s story. He was searching. He was unsaved and in a church on a Sunday morning when God broke through. So, if you’d say this morning, “I haven’t settled the issue of my sin and rebellion against God,” or “I haven’t ‘been saved,’” or “if I died on the drive home today, I wouldn’t be at peace with my Maker,” this story has a special word for you. So, let me tell you about Charlie Spurgeon. His Early and Whole Life He was born in 1834, about 40 miles northeast of London, into a Christian family. In fact, both his father and grandfather were pastors. But his father met financial troubles and sent the young Charles to live with his grandparents from ages one to six. I don’t think this is an insignificant part of the story; don’t underestimate the effects of a good grandma and grandpa in the lives of our children. From their influence he emerged as “precocious,” learned to read, and first found Bunyan’s Pilgrim’s Progress (which he would read more than a hundred times). From his earliest days, he was unusually sharp, ahead of his age level, “always reading books” (Spurgeon: A Biography, 8). He returned home at age six and excelled at school in both math and reading. content: What marks Christians attuned to cross-cultural missions? They may not serve as full-time missionaries, but they embrace Great Commission responsibilities. The history of missions reveals little-known senders who used their vocations for strategic gospel advance around the world. Captain Benjamin Wickes (1746–1830) was one such man. ‘Old Captain Wickes’ We meet this early American captain of a merchant vessel unexpectedly at a prayer meeting in 1806. The missionaries in Serampore, India, had gathered to send Henry Martyn to a station on the Ganges River where he would begin his work of translation and evangelism. Martyn recorded that they “met at my pagoda this evening for the purpose of commending me to the grace of God before my departure. My soul never before had such divine enjoyment” ( The Letters of Henry Martyn , 194). I would love to have been there. The meeting included both Baptist missionaries — William Carey, Joshua Marshman, and William Ward — as well as evangelical Anglicans David Brown, Daniel Corrie, and Henry Martyn. It represented a substantial collaboration between these earliest English missionaries for the advance of the gospel in India. Since much of India was controlled by the British East India Company, only Anglican missionaries received official recognition and freedom to travel. Even they, however, could pursue missionary work only when not employed in chaplaincy duties to English people residing in India. Amid such challenges, this prayer meeting of gathered co-laborers was a high point for Martyn and a moment he remembered fondly. To the list of those present, Martyn added “old Captain Wickes.” He mentioned him again in another letter as “the good old Captain Wickes, who has brought out so many missionaries to India” ( Letters , 178). But who was this old American captain so well loved by the English missionaries in India? Missionaries as Risky Passengers Captain Wickes was born to a seafaring family in Maryland in 1746. His older brother, Captain Lambert Wickes, fought and died at sea during the American War for Independence. Benjamin first entered the missionary record in 1799, when the Baptist missionaries Joshua Marshman and William Ward sought passage to India from London. The situation was sensitive. The East India Company had forbidden full-time missionaries from entering, so no English ship would give Marshman and Ward passage. Carey had established his home in the Danish port of Serampore, not far from Calcutta, but no Danish ships were available. Wickes’s American ship, however, could take the risk of transporting missionaries. When he heard about the situation, Wickes wrote to Baptist leader Andrew Fuller, saying that “he had long cherished the hope of being privileged to convey the messengers of the Gospel to the heathen, and that his fondest wish was about to be gratified” ( The Life and Times of Carey, Marshman, and Ward , 110). The privilege came with difficulties. Although American ships were regularly received in East India Company ports, the presence of missionaries complicated their arrival. When Wickes arrived in Calcutta with Marshman and Ward, East India Company officials refused him permission to sail home unless he took the missionaries with him. By God’s grace, Wickes convinced the authorities of the missionaries’ good intentions. When similar circumstances occurred in 1806, he persuaded officials that detaining his American ship might cause an international incident. Each voyage involved protracted negotiations that certainly distracted from his primary trading business. Yet Wickes’s service proved invaluable. Every time the missionaries mentioned him, they affirmed their unbridled thanks for his efforts. William Carey wrote about him in 1805, “I, in common with my dear brethren and sisters here, feel much pleasure in hearing of the safe return to you of our much beloved brother in Christ, Capt. 威克船长 在1806年的一次祈祷会中,我们意外地遇到了这位早期的美国商船船长. 印度塞兰波尔的传教士们聚集一堂,将亨利·马蒂恩送往恒河上的一个站,在那里他将开始翻译和福音派的工作.

Martyn记录说,他们“今晚在我的佛塔相会,目的是在我离开之前赞扬我受到上帝的恩惠。 我的灵魂从未有过如此神圣的享受”(The Letters of Henry Martyn, 194). 我很想去过那里。

与会的有浸信会传教士威廉·凯里(William Carey),约书亚·马什曼(Joshua Marshman)和威廉·沃德(William Ward)等,还有福音派圣公会教徒大卫·布朗(David Brown),丹尼尔·科里(Daniel Corrie)和亨利·马蒂恩. 它代表了这些最早的英国传教士为在印度推进福音而进行的实质性合作。

由于印度大部分地区被英国东印度公司所控制,只有英国圣公会传教士才得到官方的承认并享有出行的自由. 然而,即使他们也只能在不受雇于居住在印度的英国人担任牧师职务时才能从事传教工作。

在这样的挑战中,这次聚集的同实验室的祈祷会是马蒂恩的高潮,也是他亲切回忆的一瞬. 在出席者名单中,马蒂恩加上了“威克船长”。 他在另一封信中再次提到他,称他为“威克船长,他把这么多传教士带到了印度”(信件,178)。

但这位老美国队长 在印度的英国传教士这么爱谁? 传教士作为"冒险乘客""威克船长"于1746年生于马里兰的一个航海家庭. 他的哥哥,船长兰伯特·威克斯(Lambert Wickes)在美国独立战争中出战并死于海上.

本杰明于1799年首次入传教记录,当时浸信会传教士约书亚·马什曼和威廉·沃德从伦敦寻求通向印度. 情况很敏感。 东印度公司曾禁止全职传教士入道,因此英国船只不会给马什曼和沃德通过.

凯里在离加尔各答不远的丹麦塞兰波尔港建立了他的家,但是没有丹麦船只可供使用. 但威克斯的美国船可能承担运送传教士的风险。

当Wickes听说情况时,他写信给浸信会领袖Andrew Fuller,称“他长期以来一直珍视着有幸将福音信使传达给异教徒的希望,而且他最亲切的愿望即将得到满足”(The Life and Times of Carey, Marshman, and Ward, 110.). 特权带来了困难。

虽然美国船只经常被接收到东印度公司港口,但传教士的到来使其更加复杂. 当威克斯与马什曼和沃德一起到达加尔各答后,东印度公司官员拒绝他出航回家,除非他带着传教士一起. 在上帝的恩典下,威克说服了传教士的善意权威.

content: Participants at the IMB Sending Celebration on Nov. 9, 2026, celebrated God's faithfulness in sending 33 new missionaries to the nations. Held at the Sugarcreek campus of First Baptist Kettering near Dayton, Ohio, the event launched the State Convention of Baptists in Ohio annual gathering. For security reasons, some newly appointed missionaries are not publicly identified. IMB Photo God continues to call His people to carry the gospel to the ends of the earth. During a Sending Celebration Nov. 9 at the Sugarcreek Campus of First Baptist Church Kettering, near Dayton, Ohio, 33 International Mission Board missionaries stood before family, friends and supporters, affirming their obedience to that call. Trustees of the IMB appointed the fully supported missionaries who represent 10 states – including two candidates from Ohio – and many Southern Baptist churches committed to sending and sustaining those called by God to go to the mission field. Senior Pastor Chad Keck welcomed those in attendance, sharing his appreciation for the partnership with Southern Baptist churches to cooperatively send and support missionaries. The Sending Celebration is meeting in conjunction with the State Convention of Baptists in Ohio. Chad Keck, senior pastor of First Baptist Kettering near Dayton, Ohio, left, and Jeremy Westbrook, executive director-treasurer of the State Convention of Baptists in Ohio, right, welcome guests gathered for the IMB Sending Celebration, which kicked off the convention’s annual gathering. IMB Photo Among those who shared their stories include a couple who answered an unexpected call later in life, a couple who are returning to Albania and to people they could not forget; and a couple who moved from welcoming the nations in Canada to going to Fiji. All of them shared their stories before the Sending Celebration. Unexpected invitation to go On Dec. 5, 2025, what seemed like an ordinary FaceTime call became a turning point for Rob Boss. As he spoke with his daughter, Hannah, during her IMB training, Rob sensed God speaking clearly to his heart: “You can do this too.” The impression was unexpected. After decades of writing, Christian education, seminary teaching and active support of missions, overseas service had never been part of Rob and Stephanie Boss’ plans. “It wasn’t an audible voice, but it was so clear,” Rob said. “It was Him. It was so kind and so gentle and so encouraging.” The moment drove him to his knees in surrender. When Stephanie came home later that day, he told her he believed God was calling them to the nations. Rob’s mother served with the IMB in Africa after retirement, helping inspire Hannah’s service in South Korea. Now, three generations of the same family have answered God’s call to the nations. title_zh: IMB寻求教师、医护人员、商业专业人士担任传教士
content: IMB missionary Dr. Heidi Haun, left, checks on patients at Baptist Medical Centre in Nalerigu, Ghana. There are needed roles for IMB missionaries in healthcare, ministering to the needs of local populations and utilizing this time to minister to spiritual needs. IMB Photo When most Southern Baptists think of missionaries, they often picture church planters and evangelists. But leaders with the International Mission Board say some of the greatest needs today are for professionals whose work happens behind the scenes. IMB leaders report that critical roles such as teachers, healthcare workers, counselors, accountants, logistics specialists and member care personnel are helping advance the Great Commission in ways many churches never see. Doreen Baker, IMB director of TCK (third culture kid or missionary kid) education, sees a constant need for education professionals. Teachers are needed in international schools, which cover a variety of global educational entities, and in other settings to provide for missionary kids and their educational needs. “Teachers are significant in that not only are they providing instruction for students, but they are an integral part of the core missionary task ,” Baker said. “We also have great needs for consultants to support our families on the field with their children’s education in many ways.” Baker previously served 25 years teaching in Asia and experienced how education creates access to missions where traditional pathways may be limited. IMB missionary Ellie Bohrer teaches a 12th grade World Views class at Black Forest Academy in Germany. The IMB is seeking other educators, like Bohrer, who are willing to use their skills on the mission field. IMB Photo Scott Ray, IMB senior director of global deployment, noted that many missionary positions go unfilled simply because they fall outside traditional perceptions of missionary service. He said professional skills can provide both practical ministry support and access to countries where traditional missionary visas are difficult to obtain. Opportunities exist for finance professionals, veterinarians, medical workers, Send Relief personnel and others. Healthcare remains one of the most strategic areas in demand. Tom Hicks, IMB director of global health strategies, said many medical professionals have the wrong perception about mission work. “We do have an issue where people will select out because they don’t think that what they do is useful on the mission field,” he said. In reality, Hicks said many areas across the globe are increasingly seeking family medicine physicians, internists, pediatricians, pediatric nurse practitioners, OB providers, physical therapists, occupational therapists, speech pathologists and lactation consultants. The need is especially significant in sub-Saharan Africa, where young populations create a growing demand for pediatric care. Healthcare professionals also provide a unique advantage in countries that restrict missionary activity. “Missionaries with a vocational value, like healthcare missionaries, have opportunities to go places that others can’t go,” Hicks said. Another often-overlooked ministry is member care, which focuses on the spiritual, emotional, mental and relational health of IMB missionaries. Chris Martin is the IMB director of global member care. “Member care missionaries stand alongside those missionaries that are thought of traditionally as church planters or evangelists and support them,” Martin said. Many who serve in these roles come from counseling backgrounds and help missionaries navigate stress, conflict, grief and other challenges that can affect long-term ministry effectiveness. Martin compares their role to Aaron and Hur in Exodus 19, holding up Moses’ arms during battle, strengthening those serving on the front lines. IMB missionary Glen Garner uses his business skills and experience as the logistics director for missionaries serving globally. He lives in Lima, Peru, with his wife, Shannon

content: In South Asia, Maryam and a local pastor baptize Tara, a new believer. IMB missionaries work alongside local believers and churches to fulfill the Great Commission. IMB Photo Twenty minutes had passed already. The sun was going down, and they were looking everywhere, but they only saw men in the park. Sophia, an International Mission Board missionary, joined another IMB missionary and Maryam, a South Asian Christian. They went to the park to share the gospel, but approaching a man in their Muslim-majority city was out of the question. They kept walking and watching. Even if they went home without a single conversation, Sophia knew Maryam would want to try again. This woman who had grown up with a distrust of Muslims, now searched a park for a Muslim woman to tell about Jesus. When Sophia first invited her along, Maryam never imagined a Muslim could come to know Jesus. But the more they went out sharing the gospel together, the more God softened her heart. “One day, I found she was sharing in the park by herself, without me,” Sophia said with a laugh. These days, she shares regularly — with classmates, with rickshaw drivers, with women in the park, when she can find them. God transformed Maryam’s heart. He could transform this walk through the park, too. “So we stopped,” Sophia said, “and prayed, ‘God, give us just one woman to talk to.’” Then they spotted her — a girl sitting alone on a bench. Meeting the girl on the bench She looked like other conservative Muslim women in the area, covered in black except for her face. They approached casually, not wanting to frighten her. It was Eid al-Adha – “one of the biggest Muslim holidays here,” Sophia said. They greeted her and asked about her holiday plans. Her name was Tara, and she wasn’t intimidated at all. “You may think I’m a Muslim from the way I dress,” she said, “but actually in my heart, I have left Islam.” “I was a little shocked,” Sophia said, hearing such a bold statement from a stranger. Tara told them she was a university student at a conservative Islamic school, but she had grown disillusioned and discontent with the religion. “ I don’t believe in Islam anymore,” Tara said. Without knowledge of God, she had no one to pray to, and it left her lonely. She’d been searching — Buddhism and Hinduism from friends, even a meeting with atheists, who struck her as unhappy, following only themselves. “Do you know any Christians?” Sophia asked. “Would you like to hear what we believe?” “Sure, please share.” They read about Jesus’ birth, and Tara was hungry for more. When she asked about church, Sophia described their congregation of about 40 believers, many from a Muslim background. Though she wasn’t ready to visit the church, Tara continued her interest in learning. Sophia and Maryam met with her every week in coffee shops, tea shops, Sophia’s home, wherever they could talkthat wasn’t too loud or have “too many ears and eyes” observing them. Finding her closest friend They read through the Gospel of John. One November day in a coffee shop, they reached the passage on the Samaritan woman at the well, and Sophia noticed Tara was crying. “Tara, I see you have tears,” Sophia said. “Let’s stop. Let’s talk about it .” That day, Tara prayed to receive Christ. Soon after, she wanted to visit the church, though nervous how believers would receive her in a hijab. “They will love you,” Sophia told her. “Don’t worry.” Tara went and was welcomed. That Christmas, 80 people packed Sophia’s apartment, singing and dancing in circles. Across the room, Sophia saw Tara, wearing red Christmas garland like a scarf and a smile stretched across her face. “Tara grew up very conservative – music was not even allowed in her home. But now she’s dancing, worshiping the Lord with us with music and songs.” In South Asia, Maryam and a local pastor baptize Tara, a new believer. title_zh: 全球传教士合作伙伴通过IMB团队扩展福音工作
content: Rebeca Couto, a global missionary partner from the Azores islands, practices writing characters with her tutor in Japan. IMB Photo Rebeca Couto poses with her violin. Couto is a professional violinist who is serving as a global missionary partner with the IMB in Japan. Doors have opened for her to use her skills with evangel ical Japanese musicians who perform. IMB Photo Rebeca Couto moved from one volcanic archipelago to another, leaving Portugal’s Azores islands to anchor her life in Japan. The percentage of evangelical Christians in the Azores and Japan is similar, with both populations under 1%. Couto is a fourth-generation Christian, a rarity on the small islands. She is one of few, if any, believers in the Azores with such a long spiritual lineage. This rich legacy shaped her and prepared her for ministry. “I’ve always understood the Great Commission as a call for all believers and all disciples of Christ to be missionaries, wherever they are, whatever they’re doing, and whatever God has equipped them with,” Couto said. Couto’s great-grandfather became a Christian through the witness of missionaries from the United Kingdom. Later, missionaries from the Foreign Mission Board, now the International Mission Board, started the first Baptist work in the Azores by planting an English-speaking church near an American military base. A Baptist Brazilian couple planted a Portuguese-speaking church, which became the congregation where Couto grew up and was commissioned as a missionary. Ministry has been passed down through the generations of her family. Couto’s father has pastored for 20 years, and both of her parents have been involved in ministry for most of their lives. Couto now serves in Japan as a global missionary partner, a missionary who is financially supported by a sending church or organization in their home country and serves with IMB teams. Close to 400 GMPs currently serve on IMB teams around the world. Language learning Couto is immersed in language study in Yokohama, Japan. She had a head start before she even arrived. After graduating from high school, Couto moved from the Azores to Lisbon to pursue a degree in music. She spent hours on public transportation and wanted a challenge to pass the time. She decided to study Japanese because she thought it sounded beautiful. At the time, she had no intention of becoming a missionary in the traditional sense. However, the more she learned about the language and the culture, her burden for the lost grew. She began researching Christianity in Japan. “I understood how bleak the scenario was, and how much the country needed Jesus. I struggled with that calling because the doors were closed, and it didn’t seem possible to come to Japan for a myriad of reasons,” Couto said. After finishing master’s degrees in music and violin performance, along with a seminary degree, Couto was considering pursuing a Ph.D. or returning to seminary when her seminary professors, IMB missionaries Jonathan and Bethany Sharp, contacted her about serving as a missionary in Japan. They introduced her to the GMP program and invited her to attend a missions immersion school they piloted . Music to their ears As a professional violinist, Couto brought her violin to Japan, unsure of what opportunities existed, but she knew her call to the mission field somehow involved her gifting. “I see myself as having been called to serve through music. I never even conceived doing missions while excluding the violin entirely,” Couto said. content: IMB Graphic NASHVILLE – As the books closed on the latest fiscal year, receipts for the two Southern Baptist national annual missions offerings underscored the value Southern Baptist churches place on reaching the world with the gospel. The Lottie Moon Christmas Offering® (LMCO) totaled $212.5 million to support International Mission Board (IMB) missionaries, and the Annie Armstrong Easter Offering® (AAEO) reached $73.6 million to support the North American Mission Board’s (NAMB) church planting, compassion ministry and other evangelistic efforts to reach North America. IMB President Paul Chitwood said he celebrates what God did in the 2025-26 season and what He is doing now to lead Southern Baptists toward historic generosity. “I thank God for Southern Baptists! With giving through the Lottie Moon offering at an all-time high, churches and individual givers continue to display a heart for the gospel to be proclaimed to every nation, all tribes, peoples and languages,” Chitwood said. The Annie total marked the second highest in NAMB’s history. The record Lottie Moon offering total surpassed last year’s total by more than $5 million and is the best offering in IMB history. “God is giving our generation unprecedented opportunity to send missionaries to the most unreached peoples and places,” Chitwood continued. “Though the challenges faced by our missionaries are enormous, the generosity of Southern Baptists ensures they have what they need to face those challenges and continue in the work while we hold the ropes with our support.” IMB missionary Landon Williams (center) walks with a Chilean pastor and a U.S. pastor on a remote island in Chile. Cooperation and generosity among Southern Baptists fuels the work to reach the uttermost parts of the world with the gospel. IMB Photo National goals for both offerings are set in partnership with Woman’s Missionary Union (WMU) each year. In response to the offering totals, Sandy Wisdom-Martin, executive director-treasurer of WMU, said: “As Southern Baptists, we are all in for His mission. When we give sacrificially, we prioritize the mission of God. Together our fervent prayers, our faithful generosity and our wholehearted obedience become channels for the gospel to reach our neighbors as well as the nations.” For the last 10 years, Southern Baptists have increasingly supported the Annie offering, setting records in seven of the last 10 years. Totals in each of the last four years have surpassed $70 million. “I am so grateful to the pastors and churches for the faithfulness and generosity they have demonstrated through this offering,” said NAMB president Kevin Ezell. “As I travel and speak in churches of all sizes, I love seeing the posters in the hallways showing their offering goals. For some it is a few hundred dollars, for others several thousand.” The Annie Armstrong offering supports more than 3,000 missionaries in North America, including the ongoing work of church planting in the U.S. and Canada. In 2025, Southern Baptists planted the largest number of churches, 699, since 2016. Including church plants and replants, Southern Baptists have surpassed 700 new churches in four of the last five years. More than 12,000 churches have been planted since 2010. To go along with the increased giving totals to the SBC’s missions offerings, Southern Baptists have also increased their local outreach efforts, indicating that the focus is not just on giving but on sending. IMB Photo The chapel at Council Road Baptist Church in Oklahoma City turned into a science lab on Oct. 5-6. Microscopes, beakers and test tubes weren’t in the room, but this Sending Church Lab drew nearly 40 people representing 12 Oklahoma Baptist churches committed to send and care for international missionaries well. The Sending Church Lab, facilitated by the International Mission Board, brought pastors, church leaders and missionaries together for two days of discussion, self-assessment and planning centered on one question: What does it mean for a church to truly be a sending church? For Mike Wall, a global missions ministry partner of Oklahoma Baptists, the answer begins with churches reclaiming responsibility for the Great Commission. Wall first attended a Sending Church Lab last year in Tulsa with few expectations. He left convinced more churches needed the training. “When I went there, I thought, ‘You’ve got to do this in Oklahoma City,’” Wall said, “because of the content and how much our churches need something just like this.” After observing churches work through the exercises in the lab, Wall said he was encouraged by an emphasis on local church ownership in missions. “We can’t just send our people and say, ‘OK, now this is your job, IMB,’” he said. “We have to do our job in sending, preparing and training the best ‘sent ones’ so that when they get to the field, they can already hit the ground running.” Bryan Wooten, IMB senior church engagement specialist, leads a Sending Church Lab at Council Road Baptist Church in Oklahoma City. He is emphasizing the importance of sending churches assessing and equipping future IMB missionaries. IMB Photo Leading the lab was Bryan Wooten, IMB senior church engagement strategist, who developed the concept after seeing the need for stronger relationships between missionaries and local churches. “A Sending Church Lab is our attempt to raise up a host of IMB sending churches,” Wooten said, crediting the North American Mission Board for doing similar events and having successful results. The lab helps churches understand what Wooten calls the church engagement pathway: praying, cooperating, partnering and sending. While many churches faithfully pray, give and go, he said sending requires something more intentional. “Sending includes taking responsibility for an IMB missionary by providing ongoing encouragement, accountability and soul care throughout their term of service,” he explained. During the two-day event, participants gathered around whiteboards to evaluate their church’s missions practices, identify strengths and weaknesses and develop plans for improvement. “We don’t just need to deliver content,” Wooten said. “We need to invite churches to do some work on their own.” Rather than simply listening to presentations, attendees worked through practical questions about prayer, giving, short-term missions, missionary assessment and long-term care. Wooten said churches consistently tell him the greatest benefit is clarity. “They are thankful for clarity on what an IMB sending church is and what our roles and responsibilities are,” he said. Their real names have been changed to protect their work in Southeast Asia. “There’s no other place I’d rather be during these few days than here,” Peter said. Katie appreciated the interactive nature of the training. “I really appreciate the way they’re actually requiring information from the different churches and encouraging dialogue about how they can go through the steps,” she said. title_zh: 数字化之门为东南亚岛民打开福音之门
content: Just as young people today have become more comfortable with talking online than in person, the same is true for people in Southeast Asia. IMB missionaries are creating and publishing Jesus-focused ads, videos and other digital content to connect with the lost through the internet. IMB Photo Recently, an International Mission Board team in Southeast Asia asked a young woman if she had heard the story of Jesus. She replied that, yes, she had heard about Him through a video online! “Back in the day,” shared Amanda Clarkston, an IMB missionary who has served in Southeast Asia for 33 years, “when I first came on the field, you’d go somewhere and gather all the people together in the village to watch the JESUS film.” Now, face-to-face conversations about Christ on the Southeast Asian islands are harder to accomplish. While teams travel to these remote islands often, living in a sparsely populated, animistic background culture as a foreigner creates suspicion and make long-term ministry difficult. Furthermore, young people today have become more comfortable with talking online than they are in person, Clarkston said, which is true of the islanders as well. Attempting to have a spiritual conversation face-to-face has become “too much” for locals, Clarkston shared. So, how do you share the gospel with multiple people groups who are constantly online and less comfortable with in-person interactions? For these Southeast Asia teams, digital engagement — the use of social media platforms to share a message — has become a plausible and effective entry point. The social media agency We Are Social confirmed this, revealing that 82.4% of Southeast Asia’s population uses the internet. “No matter where they go, how far they go, how remote it is, people have phones,” Clarkston and her team realized, “And though sometimes they do have to climb up the highest peak to get reception, people do it.” Clarkston’s team has begun creating and publishing Jesus-focused ads, videos and other digital content in hopes of building bridges to the islanders through the internet. Viewers can click on the ad to message back and forth with a responder, a local believer or missionary who is available to pray, build relationships and answer spiritual questions. “It seems like locals are more open to watching those things in the privacy of their own cell phones,” Clarkston said. Clarkston intends to use digital engagement as a means for initial contact with people with animistic backgrounds, evangelism and, eventually, discipleship. She said that this new ministry has the potential to open doors with individuals across these islands who would normally never reach out on their own or respond to the gospel in person. “Maybe they’ll respond this way,” Clarkston said, “I know without a shadow of a doubt that God is calling people to Himself.” Now, more than ever, technology has a grip on society. Many spend hours each day mindlessly scrolling, searching for meaning, for happiness. And now, more than ever, there is an incredible opportunity to plant seeds across Southeast Asian islands through digital engagement. The IMB Southeast Asia team gives praise to the Lord that He has provided a creative way to reach the lost and plant seeds. Pray the people among the Southeast Asian islands would see these ads and engage with responders boldly, even though they may face persecution or harm because of it. Names were changed for security. content: Ask most people what comes to mind when they think of South Korea, and they’ll likely mention K-pop, skincare, cutting-edge technology, or bustling city streets filled with young professionals. Hun and Eunjoo Sol see those things too. But after more than a decade serving as International Mission Board missionaries in Seoul, they also see something many visitors never notice. “Many people think that Korea is exciting and successful,” Hun said. “They think about the K-pop, the K-culture, K-technology, K-cosmetics. Yes, good things… But many Korean people are struggling right now.” The Sols, who were featured in the 2025 Week of Prayer for International Missions , continue to rely on the prayers of faithful Southern Baptists. Prayers sustain them and help to push back the darkness they confront in their home culture. Hun often describes that hidden struggle with a Korean word: han. There is no simple English translation. It speaks to a deep sorrow shaped by generations of war, division, loss, and the quiet resolve to endure. Hun sees it in the young adults he meets every week—people navigating loneliness and relentless expectations, quietly asking what their lives are for beneath a veneer of success. Han is heavy. For many young adults, that weight can feel unbearable. Suicide is one of the leading causes of death among teenagers and young adults in South Korean. Hun and Eunjoo see the effects of that reality every day, and it’s one reason they believe they have no time to waste. That understanding shaped the week of Serve Tour Seoul this summer. There were no construction sites, no paintbrushes, no tools or work gloves. Instead, the team stepped into ministries local churches had been faithfully building long before the volunteers arrived. In May, 27 volunteers from seven churches across the United States came alongside local churches already serving their communities in Seoul, Paju, and Gwangju. They taught English classes, ran children’s camps, walked neighborhoods in prayer, distributed food, and sat down with college students, one conversation at a time. For Nick Holst of Sandals Church in Riverside, California, the goal was simple enough to say in a sentence: “We came to meet people,” Holst said. “We want to hear their stories, and that leads to some very meaningful connections as you get past the surface into something deeper.” That’s where the week actually lived: past the surface and past the small talk, where the quiet weight of han is often carried without words. On college campuses, volunteers played games, asked questions and mostly just listened. Some conversations lasted a few minutes and ended there. Others kept going long past the point where either person expected them to. One morning, after asking his church back home to pray, Holst sat down with a university student named Intec. They talked about culture first, the way strangers do, and then the conversation turned somewhere neither of them planned. “I got to ask him, ‘What do Koreans believe?’” Holst recalled. Intec said he didn’t believe in God. Then he recited John 3:16 from memory, word for word, a verse he’d heard somewhere along the way and never forgotten. Before they parted, Holst asked if he could pray that God would keep drawing Intec toward Himself. “He said yes.” In a city where many conversations never move beyond the surface, the exchange was a reminder of why the team had come. Not to win an argument, but to listen, to ask questions, and to trust God with what happens next. The same pattern unfolded elsewhere, beginning in classrooms and ending on city streets. Jeremy Doyle, missions pastor at Valley Baptist Church in Bakersfield, California, watched an English conversation club grow from two students on its first night to eight by the second. Brown here draws attention to a practice that was gaining ground in the churches of his day: that of holding ‘amusements’ of various kinds, which obscured, diverted from, and in some cases replaced the proper ministry of local churches. Brown was savagely attacked in the wake of the publication of the pamphlet, derided as ‘a kill-joy,’ ‘a morbid pietist,’ and ‘a sour bigot.’ His meaning, however, had been deliberately misrepresented. 1 Brown nowhere objects to all amusement per se , but amusement which masquerades as ministry, distracting the church and deceiving needy sinners. While the context in which Brown wrote may be different from ours, we need to hear his burden for a Church—and for Christians—to make a decisive break with the world and its practices. An Evil in the Camp of the Lord DIFFERENT days demand their own special testimony. The watchman who would be faithful to his Lord and the City of his God has need to carefully note the signs of the times and emphasize his witness accordingly. Con­cerning the testimony needed now, there can the little, if any, doubt. An evil is in the professed camp of the Lord—so gross, so brazen in its impudence—that the most short-sighted of spiritual men can hardly fail to notice it. During the past few years it has developed at an ab­normal rate, ever for evil. It has worked like leaven until now the whole lump ferments. Look which way you may, its presence makes itself manifest. There is little if any­thing, to choose between Church, Chapel, or Mission Hall. However they may differ in some respects, they bear a striking likeness in the posters that figure upon and dis­figure their notice boards. Amusement for the people i s the leading article advertised by each. If any of my readers doubt my statement, or think my utterance too sweeping, let them take a tour of inspection and study “the announce­ments for the week” at the doors of the sanctuaries of the neighbourhood; or let them read the religious advertise­ments in their local papers. I have done this again and again, until the hideous fact has been proved up to the hilt, that “amusement” is ousting the preaching of the gospel as the great attraction: “Concerts,” “Entertain­ments,” “Fancy Fairs,” “Smoking Conferences,” “Dramatic Performances,” are the words honoured with biggest type and most startling colours.
